No new ideas today: you balance one game with what you learned in Lecture
16. Do each activity alone, then open "Check your result". Every question on
this page has its answer: try first, then check.

## Recall

- P(at least one drop in n tries) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ; the average is 1/p tries.
- A pity timer limits the longest wait.
- The expected reward E = Σ value × probability; chests for an item ≈
  price ÷ E.
- Independent tries have no memory; a shuffle bag gives exact shares.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Recall"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="2|100 %"}
p = 0.5. P(at least one drop in 2 tries)?
:   3/4

    Why: 1 − (1/2)².

p = 0.1. How many tries on average?
:   10

    Why: 1/p.

A chest: 50 % 2 coins, 50 % 8 coins. E?
:   5

    Why: 1 + 4.
:::
:::

## Activity 1 · How many attacks to win?

*Mole Keep* is a small fighting game. The **hits needed** are health ÷
damage, rounded up. With hit chance h, the **expected attacks** are hits ÷ h.
The side that needs fewer attacks usually wins.

![Expected attacks for three enemies.](images/difficulty.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 1 · Expected attacks · 10 min"}
The player has 50 health, 10 damage and the hit chance 0.5. A goblin has 30
health, 10 damage and the hit chance 0.5.

1. How many hits does the player need to beat the goblin? How many attacks
   on average?
2. How many attacks does the goblin need to beat the player?
3. The designer gives the goblin 25 damage. Who is in danger now?

*Your product:* four numbers and one sentence.

::: {.check}
1. 30 ÷ 10 = 3 hits; 3 ÷ 0.5 = **6 attacks**. 2. 50 ÷ 10 = 5 hits; 5 ÷ 0.5 =
**10 attacks**: the player usually wins. 3. 50 ÷ 25 = 2 hits; 2 ÷ 0.5 = **4
attacks**: now the goblin needs fewer attacks than the player (6), so the
player is in danger.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Attacks"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="2|12"}
Health 40, damage 15. How many hits?
:   3

    Why: 40 ÷ 15 = 2.7, rounded up.

4 hits needed, hit chance 0.5. Expected attacks?
:   8

    Why: 4 ÷ 0.5.

5 hits needed, hit chance 1. Expected attacks?
:   5

    Why: every attack hits.
:::
:::

## Activity 2 · Tune an enemy

A normal enemy should be beaten in **70–85 %** of the fights, a boss in
**30–45 %**. **Difficulty Tuner** simulates 1000 fights.

{{< sim file="sims/difficulty-tuner.html" poster="sims/difficulty-tuner.png" title="Difficulty Tuner: how hard is the skeleton?" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 2 · Normal enemy and boss · 12 min"}
1. Simulate the skeleton (40 health, 12 damage, 60 % hit). What is the
   player's win rate? Is it a normal enemy?
2. Change **one** value so that the skeleton is a normal enemy. Write it.
3. Change values until it is a boss. Write them.

*Your product:* one win rate and two sets of values with their win rates.

::: {.check}
1. About 88 %: too easy for a normal enemy. 2. For example damage 16: about
73 %. 3. A good answer has a win rate from 30 to 45 %, for example more
health and more damage. Check: you changed one value at a time and
simulated after each change.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Tuning"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="change all values at once|95 %"}
Which win rate fits a normal enemy?
:   78 %

    Why: it is inside 70–85 %.

Which win rate fits a boss?
:   40 %

    Why: it is inside 30–45 %.

How should a designer change the numbers?
:   one value at a time, then simulate

    Why: then you know what made the difference.
:::
:::

## Activity 3 · Simulate 1000 players

A formula gives the average; a simulation also shows the unlucky players.
**Drop Rate Lab** lets 1000 players hunt a rare item.

![A pity timer.](images/pity-timer.png){width=80%}

{{< sim file="sims/drop-rate-lab.html" poster="sims/drop-rate-lab.png" title="Drop Rate Lab: how long do players wait?" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 3 · The rare hammer · 12 min"}
A rare hammer drops with p = 2 %.

1. What is the average number of tries? Compute it, then check in the lab.
2. Simulate 1000 players without a pity timer. What is the longest wait?
3. Add a pity timer at 60. What are the average and the longest wait now?

*Your product:* one computed and three simulated numbers, and one sentence:
would you keep the timer?

::: {.check}
1. 1/0.02 = **50 tries**. 2. The longest wait is often 200 or more: some
players wait very long. 3. The average falls a little (to about 40), and
the longest wait is **60**. A good sentence: keep the timer, because it
ends the endless waits but keeps early lucky drops.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Simulations"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="the average only|0"}
p = 2 %. The average number of tries?
:   50

    Why: 1/p = 1 ÷ 0.02.

Pity timer at 60. The longest wait?
:   60

    Why: try 60 always gives the item.

What does a simulation show that the formula 1/p does not?
:   the unlucky players

    Why: it shows the whole spread of waits, not only the average.
:::
:::

## Activity 4 · Input or output randomness?

**Input randomness** happens before the player decides (a random map, the
cards in hand); the player can plan around it. **Output randomness** decides
the result after the decision (a hit roll, a random reward).

![Input and output randomness.](images/input-output.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 4 · Sort the luck · 10 min"}
1. Sort into input or output: a random dungeon map; the damage roll of an
   attack; the cards dealt at the start; a random reward after a level; the
   weather shown before a race.
2. *Mole Keep* decides every fight with one roll after the player attacks.
   Players say "skill does not matter". Suggest one change to input
   randomness.

*Your product:* two lists and one change.

::: {.check}
1. Input: the map, the cards at the start, the weather before the race.
Output: the damage roll, the reward after the level. 2. A good change moves
luck before the decision, for example random enemy positions that the
player sees before choosing a path; the fight itself depends more on the
player's choices.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Input or output?"}
Choose the right answer. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="neither"}
The tiles of a puzzle before the player moves.
:   input

    Why: the player sees them and plans.

The roll that decides if an attack hits.
:   output

    Why: it decides the result after the choice.

A random prize after the level.
:   output

    Why: it comes after the player's decisions.
:::
:::

## Activity 5 · Honest odds

A chest of *Mole Keep* uses the weights common 80, rare 15, epic 5, and an
epic is guaranteed after 30 chests without one. The store page says "epic
10 %".

![The chances of a chest.](../week-12/images/weighted.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 5 · The chest screen · 10 min"}
1. What is the real chance of an epic in one chest? Is the store page
   honest?
2. Write the three odds the chest screen must show.
3. Write one sentence that tells players about the pity timer.

*Your product:* one answer, three odds and one sentence.

::: {.check}
1. 5/100 = **5 %**: the page says 10 %, so it is not honest. 2. Common 80 %,
rare 15 %, epic 5 %. 3. For example: "If you open 30 chests without an epic,
the next one is an epic."
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · Honest odds"}
Weights 80, 15, 5. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="20 %|10 %"}
What must the screen show for rare?
:   15 %

    Why: 15 ÷ 100.

The code uses 5 % for epic, the page says 10 %. What is this?
:   dishonest odds

    Why: shown odds must be the real odds.

Why tell players about a pity timer?
:   so they know the real rule

    Why: honest odds include how drops really work.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note .ai-task title="Task with AI · Simulate 1000 hunters"}
**Goal:** a spreadsheet that lets 1000 players hunt the rare hammer (p = 2 %)
and shows the average and the longest wait. It is far beyond hand work; an
AI assistant writes the formulas, and you check them with what you know.

1. **Ask the AI:** start with this prompt.

   ::: {.prompt}
   I use a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets). Each row is one player who
   tries again and again until a rare item drops, with the chance 2 % per
   try. Write one formula that gives the number of tries for one player,
   using a random number. Then write formulas for the average and the
   largest value of 1000 rows.
   :::

2. **Do it yourself:** fill 1000 rows and read the average and the largest
   value. Then change 2 % to 5 %.
3. **Check:** the average must be close to 1/p (50 tries, then 20). Compare
   the largest value with Drop Rate Lab. A value of 0 tries, or an average
   far from 1/p, means a wrong formula.

*Your product:* the sheet, the averages for 2 % and 5 %, and one sentence
on what the AI got wrong or what you changed.

::: {.check}
A good sheet: 1000 rows; the average near 50 (2 %) and near 20 (5 %); the
largest value often over 200 for 2 %; no row with 0 tries. AI formulas often
forget to round up (and give 0 tries) or use the chance of a miss and of a
drop the wrong way round: look for both.
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Fair or Frustrating? {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every activity of today.

The *Torch Hall* team reads six messages. A player hits with **80 %** and
missed **two times in a row**. Another rolled **no 6 in five rolls**. A key
drops with **50 %**, and a player tried **three times**. Crits come with
**20 %** from a **shuffle bag with 1 crit and 4 normal hits**. A chest gives
**10 coins (80 %) or 50 coins (20 %)**, and a bow costs **180 coins**.

{{< sim file="sims/fair-or-frustrating.html" poster="sims/fair-or-frustrating.png" title="Fair or Frustrating? Messages about luck" kind="game" height="440" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7 · Balance the messages (harder)"}
Hit 80 %; key 50 %; bag 1 crit + 4 normal; chest 10 (80 %) or 50 (20 %),
bow 180. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="input|250"}
Is the hit roll of 80 % input or output randomness?
:   output

    Why: it decides the result after the attack.

1000 players try for the key 3 times. About how many have none?
:   125

    Why: (1/2)³ = 1/8 of 1000.

The key gets a pity timer at try 3. The longest wait?
:   3 tries

    Why: try 3 always gives the key.

4 hits needed with the hit chance 80 %. Expected attacks?
:   5

    Why: 4 ÷ 0.8.

What must the chest screen show?
:   80 % and 20 %

    Why: honest odds are the real ones.
:::
:::

## Wrap-up {.summary}

- You can compute the expected attacks of a fight and say who usually wins.
- You can tune an enemy and a drop rate with simulations of many players.
- You can sort input and output randomness and suggest a fairer change.
- You can write the honest odds of a chest.
